title: What can you say about ashwagandha in your ads and on your site?
summary: The library supports 3 wordings for ashwagandha; the strongest is "Used in herbal medicine as an adaptogen: helps the body build resistance to stress and supports energy over time, for example when stress leaves you mentally and physically tired" (moderate, 2.5-6.5 g dried root or whole plant (or extract equivalent) a day). Avoid wording that names or implies a disease, a drug or a treatment, such as "Treats anxiety or depression".

supported_wordings.wording: Used in herbal medicine as an adaptogen: helps the body build resistance to stress and supports energy over time, for example when stress leaves you mentally and physically tired.
supported_wordings.why: Health Canada lists it, and ODS reports trials in which ashwagandha lowered stress and anxiety scores, but the two describe different forms and doses.
supported_wordings.daily_dose: 2.5-6.5 g dried root or whole plant (or extract equivalent) a day
supported_wordings.dose_details: Adults 18 and older, per Health Canada. The trials ODS describes used 240-1,250 mg of extract a day, a different measure.
supported_wordings.form: Dried, powdered or ethanolic extract of root or whole plant

sources.name: NIH ODS fact sheet: Ashwagandha (health professional)

supported_wordings.wording: Traditionally used in Ayurveda to ease restlessness and nervousness, which helps support sleep.
supported_wordings.why: Traditional use only in Health Canada's monograph; ODS reports some trials with better sleep quality in stressed adults, using different extracts and doses.
supported_wordings.daily_dose: 2-6 g dried root (or extract equivalent) a day
supported_wordings.dose_details: Adults 18 and older. The claim names the tradition (Ayurveda).
supported_wordings.form: Dried or powdered root, or ethanol and/or water extracts

sources.name: NIH ODS fact sheet: Ashwagandha (health professional)

supported_wordings.wording: Traditionally used in Ayurveda as a rejuvenating tonic and to support memory.
supported_wordings.why: Traditional use only, per Health Canada.
supported_wordings.daily_dose: 2-6 g dried root (or extract equivalent) a day
supported_wordings.dose_details: Adults 18 and older. The claim names the tradition (Ayurveda).
supported_wordings.form: Dried or powdered root, or ethanol and/or water extracts

wordings_to_avoid.why: Names mental health disorders; the supported wording is about resistance to everyday stress.
Names a sleep disorder and promises a cure.

wordings_to_avoid.wording: Works like an antidepressant or anti-anxiety drug
wordings_to_avoid.why: Compares the product to a drug class.

wordings_to_avoid.wording: Raises low testosterone, or treats low T
wordings_to_avoid.why: Low testosterone as a diagnosis is a medical condition; no listed source supports a testosterone claim.
Names a disease; ODS flags thyroid effects as a safety concern, not a benefit.

evidence_strengths.strong: At least two listed sources support it independently at a comparable dose and form, and none disagrees.
evidence_strengths.moderate: One listed source supports it as an evidence-based use at that dose, and no listed source disagrees.
evidence_strengths.limited: The only support is traditional use, the sources disagree, or the source itself calls the evidence weak.

reasons_to_avoid.drug: names a drug or presents the product as one
reasons_to_avoid.treatment: promises to treat, cure or prevent a condition

sources.name: NIH ODS fact sheet: Ashwagandha (health professional)

disclaimer: Not legal advice. This guide shows the wording that published evidence supports at a daily dose, from the sources linked below; it is not a ruling on any claim. Your own product, its form and dose, and your own evidence still need to match the wording you use.
